config.title: Network security

intro.title: Network security
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple network security simulator that demonstrates how firewalls filter incoming connections. You will learn to implement basic packet filtering logic by checking connection requests against security rules. The core programming concept involves using conditional statements to make security decisions based on source and destination data. You will work with fundamental security constructs like allow/deny rules and port validation. This hands-on exercise will help you understand how network security controls traffic flow in real-world systems.
intro.usecase: Network security principles are foundational to every web application that handles user data or sensitive operations. Developers implement these concepts when building secure login forms, encrypted payment dashboards, and admin panels that require authentication and authorization. For example, a banking app's transaction interface uses network security to encrypt data in transit and validate user sessions, while an e-commerce checkout securely transmits credit card details. Understanding these patterns is essential for creating features like secure API calls, protected user profiles, and compliance with data protection regulations in real-world products.

objectives: Implement a basic firewall rule to filter network traffic
Configure secure network protocols for data transmission
Construct a network monitoring system to detect suspicious activity
Apply encryption techniques to protect data in transit
Initialize a secure network connection with proper authentication
Manipulate network access controls to restrict unauthorized users
Integrate security headers into network communications

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and the useState hook.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The necessary React dependencies are imported for managing state in the network security component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to import both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Please import React and useState from 'react' to proceed.

steps.title: Create the NetworkSecurity component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named NetworkSecurity that returns an empty fragment.
steps.hint: Define the component using either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. Return React.Fragment (<> </>) or null.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';
// Create the NetworkSecurity component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A NetworkSecurity component is defined and returns an empty fragment.
successCriteria: The component is named NetworkSecurity and returns an empty fragment (<> </>) or null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a component, but ensure it's named exactly NetworkSecurity and returns an empty fragment.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Create a functional component named NetworkSecurity that returns an empty fragment.

steps.title: Initialize state for security status
steps.instruction: Inside your NetworkSecurity component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'isSecure' and initialize it to false.
steps.hint: Call useState with the initial value false and destructure the returned array into isSecure and setIsSecure.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: state for a toggle
const [isOn, setIsOn] = useState(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable isSecure that tracks whether the network is secure, starting as false.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with false, and the destructured variable is named isSecure.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with false and naming the variable isSecure.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use useState(false) and destructure to get isSecure and setIsSecure.

steps.title: Define toggle security handler
steps.instruction: Inside the NetworkSecurity component, define a function called toggleSecurity that toggles the isSecure state between true and false.
steps.hint: Create a function that uses the setter function from useState to update the state to the opposite of its current value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The toggleSecurity function should be defined inside the component and use the setter function to toggle the isSecure state.
successCriteria: A function named toggleSecurity is defined that toggles the isSecure state value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function uses the setter to toggle the boolean state value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggleSecurity function isn't defined correctly. It should toggle the isSecure state between true and false.

steps.title: Define detect threat handler
steps.instruction: Inside your NetworkSecurity component, define a function called detectThreat that increments the threatCount state by 1.
steps.hint: You'll need to use the setThreatCount function to update the state. The function should take no parameters and increase the count by 1.
steps.expectedOutcome: A detectThreat function is added to your component that properly increments the threatCount state.
successCriteria: The detectThreat function is defined and uses setThreatCount to increment the threatCount state by 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your detectThreat function properly increments the threatCount state by 1 using setThreatCount.
steps.feedbackWrong: The detectThreat function isn't defined correctly. It should increment the threatCount state by 1 when called.

steps.title: Add main container and security status display
steps.instruction: In your NetworkSecurity component's return statement, replace the current 'return null;' with a main container div. Inside this div, add a heading that says 'Network Security Dashboard' and a paragraph that displays the current security status based on the isSecure state.
steps.hint: The paragraph should use the isSecure state variable to conditionally display 'Secure' or 'Insecure'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a structured UI with a heading and a paragraph that dynamically shows the security status.
successCriteria: The return statement contains a div with an h1 and a p element. The paragraph uses the isSecure state to display 'Secure' or 'Insecure'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some structure, but make sure the paragraph correctly displays 'Secure' or 'Insecure' based on the isSecure state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The return statement doesn't yet contain the required div, heading, and dynamic paragraph. Review the instruction and try again.

steps.title: Add threat count display
steps.instruction: Inside your NetworkSecurity component's return statement, add a paragraph element that displays the current threatCount value. Use the format: 'Threats detected: X' where X is the threatCount state value.
steps.hint: Use JSX curly braces to embed the threatCount state variable inside the paragraph text.
steps.analogousExample:
// Displaying a state value in JSX

Current count: {count}
steps.expectedOutcome: A paragraph element showing 'Threats detected: ' followed by the current threatCount value appears in the component's output.
successCriteria: The component returns a paragraph element containing the text 'Threats detected: ' and the threatCount state value inside JSX curly braces.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your paragraph shows both the text 'Threats detected: ' and the actual threatCount value using JSX curly braces.
steps.feedbackWrong: The threat count display isn't quite right. Check that you've added a paragraph element with the correct text format and embedded the threatCount state variable.

steps.title: Add toggle security button and wire handler
steps.instruction: Add a button element with the text 'Toggle Security' inside the main container. Wire its onClick event to call the toggleSecurity handler.
steps.hint: Use the <button> tag with onClick={toggleSecurity} and place it after the existing paragraphs.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding an interactive button
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Toggle Security' appears in the UI that will trigger the toggleSecurity handler when clicked.
successCriteria: The button element with text 'Toggle Security' is present and its onClick event is correctly wired to the toggleSecurity handler.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but make sure it has the correct text and onClick handler.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or not properly configured. Check the instruction again.

steps.title: Add detect threat button and wire handler
steps.instruction: Add a button element with the text 'Detect Threat' inside the main container, and wire its onClick event to call the detectThreat handler.
steps.hint: Add a <button> element after the existing toggle button. Use onClick={detectThreat} to connect it to your handler.

<button onClick={handleAction}>Perform Action</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will now have a 'Detect Threat' button that, when clicked, will trigger the detectThreat handler function.
successCriteria: A button with text 'Detect Threat' is added to the component's return statement, and its onClick event is properly wired to the detectThreat handler.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but it's missing either the correct text or the onClick handler. Make sure it says 'Detect Threat' and calls detectThreat when clicked.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button element is missing or incorrectly implemented. Add a <button> with text 'Detect Threat' and onClick={detectThreat} inside the main container.
